purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for P17–P22, the six rhythm and emphasis drafts. Fields remain outside strict Commons frontmatter.

articles.title: Vary Sentence Length Deliberately
use_when: Sentences have a mechanically uniform movement despite changes in thought.
A discovery receives the same weight as routine background or action.
The passage needs a deliberate relationship between continuing, qualifying, and stopping.
mechanisms: Grouping related material into continuous movement
Creating contrast through changes of length and structure
Matching sentence shape to its contribution in context
not_ideal_when: Uniformity deliberately supports routine, comparison, pressure, or usability.
A forced length change would obscure the logic or become a predictable dramatic formula.
example_user_queries: Every sentence in my paragraph sounds the same.
A discovery in my scene feels like one more routine action.
Do shorter sentences always make the pace faster?
I alternate long and short sentences but the writing still feels mechanical.
How can I join background to a claim without burying the point?
My short sentences seem to slow the scene down.
I want a deliberate routine rather than random variety.
Should I aim for a particular average sentence length?
My paragraphs all end with a tiny dramatic sentence and the effect feels repetitive.
How do I hear where a passage needs to continue or stop?

sources.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
sources.title: Book View Cafe: Navigating the Ocean of Story: Session 1, Part 5
sources.inspected_material: The question from Linda and Le Guin's answer on sentence length as one element of pacing, variety, appropriateness, and contextual fit.
sources.supports: Using varied lengths suited to what a sentence says and its context, without treating short sentences as a general pacing rule.
sources.limits: No full book passage, quoted advice, fixed word threshold, or empirical reading-time claim is adopted. The rehearsal and workshop situations are original.

sources.author: Purdue OWL, Purdue University

sources.inspected_material: The introductory guidance and the discussion of rhythm, length, structure, and emphasis.
sources.supports: Considering sentence structure and length as related choices that can alter rhythm and emphasis.
sources.limits: No source exercise is reproduced and no mandatory alternation or claim that every repeated form is monotonous is adopted. The original comparisons do not isolate word count experimentally.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons show the relevant metaphor, inference, or change of sentence movement directly. A separate table or graphic would detach the choices from their context; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Put Weight at the End
use_when: A sentence's main development loses force under trailing procedural detail.
The same facts need a different emphasis for this paragraph's purpose.
A final qualification must be retained but its placement obscures the intended arrival.
mechanisms: Arranging a sentence toward its intended arrival
Moving attribution and secondary context without erasing them
Giving paragraph details a relevant point of closure
not_ideal_when: Readers need an immediate answer or instruction before any build-up.
A revised ending would delete a material qualification or distort an established sequence.
example_user_queries: My important point is buried before a tail of background detail.
A sentence says the right thing but seems to end on the wrong thing.
How can I emphasize the decision without removing its source?
The paragraph loses its force in the last sentence.
Should the most important information always go last?
A qualification at the end is necessary but makes the sentence awkward.
I want the reader to arrive at a consequence rather than a meeting date.
Can passive voice help place the information I want to emphasize?
My cancellation notice takes too long to give the actual news.
How do I make a quiet paragraph ending meaningful without inventing a dramatic twist?

sources.author: Duke Graduate School Scientific Writing Resource

sources.supports: Considering final position as a useful place to arrange information intended to receive emphasis.
sources.limits: The society update, translator scene, and notice are original hypothetical examples. No scientific exercise, universal reading response, quantified memory benefit, or full book passage is adopted. Paragraph closure and answer-first alternatives are editorial extensions.

articles.title: Use Parallel Form for Related Ideas
use_when: Related ideas change grammatical footing within a comparison or series.
Descriptions of options leave the reader to discover which features correspond.
Matching forms risk hiding unequal responsibilities or evidence.
mechanisms: Matching grammatical shapes to related contributions
Making each element fit a shared construction
Preserving distinctions of agency and evidential status within correspondence
not_ideal_when: The situations do not warrant the implied equivalence.
A deliberately unsettled exchange would be misrepresented by composed symmetry.
example_user_queries: My comparison describes different features of each option.
A list changes shape halfway through and readers lose track.
How can I make two positions easier to compare without pretending they are equal?
The sentence is grammatical but its comparison still feels uneven.
One item in my list does not fit the opening phrase.
Do parallel phrases need the same number of words?
A neat rewrite has hidden who is responsible for each action.
Can matching sentence forms express two characters' different concerns?
I have a confirmed quote for one option and only a guess for the other.
Does parallel structure require repeating the same words?

sources.supports: Using grammatical correspondence for related elements at several scales and making each element fit its construction.

articles.title: Repeat with a Purpose
use_when: A repeated phrase could gather force as distinct contributions accumulate.
Replacing recurring labels makes continuity harder to follow.
The same words acquire a new role as a local exchange develops.
mechanisms: Holding wording steady while context or contribution changes
Using repeated beginnings to connect related statements
Maintaining a clear established label across instructions
not_ideal_when: Recurrence restates an effect already complete without adding orientation or pressure.
A repeated accusation would flatten materially different facts into a misleading pattern.
example_user_queries: I keep replacing repeated words and the writing starts to sound unnatural.
How can a repeated phrase build pressure without becoming redundant?
A key term needs to stay recognizable through several instructions.
I want the reader to hear that these separate requests have something in common.
Can the same words mean something different later in a conversation?
My email sounds like a speech because every sentence starts the same way.
How many times should I repeat a phrase?
I cannot tell whether a recurring sentence adds force or just takes up space.
A strong repeated accusation may oversimplify what actually happened.
What should change around a repeated phrase to keep the passage developing?

sources.author: Ursula K. Le Guin, in Hachette UK's Gollancz Festival Q&A
sources.title: Ursula K. Le Guin – Answers your questions for Gollancz Festival 2015
sources.inspected_material: Keegan Spindler's question and Le Guin's answer distinguishing deliberate repetition from carelessness, including names and pronouns needed for clarity.
sources.supports: Retaining useful recurrence rather than automatically replacing repeated wording and attending to its purpose during revision.
sources.limits: No quoted answer or full Steering the Craft passage is reproduced. The booking, studio, and restaurant situations are original; no universal benefit is asserted.

articles.title: Punctuate for Pace and Meaning
use_when: Punctuation makes a qualification, explanation, or interruption read with the wrong relationship.
The writer follows imagined breath without clarifying clause boundaries.
A narrative fragment or aside needs an intentional place in the sentence's movement.
mechanisms: Choosing boundaries according to clause relationships
Distinguishing continuation from specification and interruption
Making fragments intelligible through available context
not_ideal_when: Additional marks would preserve an overloaded sentence that needs rebuilding.
A punctuation change would demote a material limit or obscure which group a claim concerns.
example_user_queries: The words are right but the sentence moves in the wrong way.
Should these statements be joined by a semicolon, a colon, or a full stop?
I use dashes for every qualification and the prose feels overdramatic.
I put commas where I breathe but my sentences are still confusing.
A change of punctuation seems to change which people the sentence is about.
How do I make an aside secondary without hiding something important?
Can a sentence fragment work in a narrative?
I keep adding marks to a sentence that may need to be split.
A report makes a routine qualification sound like a big revelation.
How can punctuation show the relationship rather than just create pauses?

sources.author: Purdue OWL, Purdue University
sources.title: Brief Overview of Punctuation
sources.inspected_material: Definitions of independent and dependent clauses and the sections on comma boundaries, semicolons, colons, parentheses, and dashes.
sources.supports: Choosing conventional punctuation according to grammatical relationships and the placement or emphasis of related material.
sources.limits: The hall update, courtyard comparison, and student scene are original hypothetical examples. No source exercise, fixed pause duration, comprehensive rulebook, or universal hierarchy of emotional effects is adopted. Fragment and contextual-emphasis comparisons are editorial development.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose passages show clause relationships, formal departures, and differences in perceptual selection directly. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Break an Established Form for Emphasis
use_when: An important contrast passes like another item in a series.
A passage has an identifiable verbal or grammatical baseline that a turn can depart from.
A proposed emphasis needs to be distinguished from merely adding surprising information.
mechanisms: Changing grammatical roles or sentence type at a relevant turn
Judging a departure relative to what the passage has prepared
not_ideal_when: No actual baseline exists or the change is only a new fact in the same form.
Manufactured regularity would distort the facts, voice, or usability of the passage.
example_user_queries: My decisive contrast reads like one more item in the list.
How can I use a repeated sentence shape to give a turn more force?
I call this a pattern break but I cannot identify the pattern.
The event is surprising but the form of the prose has not changed.
Can a shift from statements to a question create emphasis?
I have made the earlier sentences too neat just to set up the ending.
Every paragraph in my draft builds a pattern and then snaps into a fragment.
How many repetitions are needed before a departure becomes noticeable?
A rhetorical question makes the problem look fatal without considering answers.
The formal symmetry sounds too composed for my narrator's current state.
